Here is a problem from another field that shares the underlying structure of the research question below, with notes on how that field investigates it.

<parallel>
Field: Computer engineering (hardware)
Problem: Verifying that a circuit element such as a flip-flop, SRAM cell or memristor holds a state after the input signal that set it is removed, and that this state later changes its output.
How it is studied: Engineers apply write pulses, remove them, then read the state repeatedly over time to measure retention and decay. They sweep inputs to map bistability and hysteresis in the transfer curve. Stress tests with noise, temperature and repeated cycling show how reliable and durable the stored state is.
</parallel>

Each of your ideas must transfer a specific method, measurement logic, or principle from how that field studies its problem, while still being a concrete, scientifically sound way to address the research question.

Research question: "What analyses or measurements would best test whether AP-1 acts as a cellular memory mechanism?"

Propose 5 distinct, concrete ideas (analyses, measurements, or experiments) that a research lab could pursue to address this question. For each idea give a short title and a description of one or two sentences.

ideas.title: Write-remove-read retention assay for AP-1 chromatin state
ideas.description: Apply a transient stimulus (e.g., a defined pulse of TPA, a growth factor, or optogenetic c-Fos/c-Jun activation), then wash it out. Track AP-1 binding (CUT&RUN), chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq) and target gene expression at timepoints from hours to many cell divisions. Retention is shown if accessibility and output persist after AP-1 activity itself has decayed to baseline.

ideas.title: Dose-sweep hysteresis mapping of AP-1 targets
ideas.description: Ramp stimulus intensity up and then down in separate cell populations. Use single-cell readouts such as a reporter or scRNA-seq for AP-1 target output at each step. If the up and down response curves differ, with bimodal populations at intermediate doses, the system has hysteresis and bistability, which are signatures of memory rather than simple tracking of input.

ideas.title: Read-out test: does the stored state change later responses?
ideas.description: After a priming pulse and washout, challenge primed and naive cells with a second stimulus. Compare the speed, amplitude and gene set of the response, including whether it needs AP-1 or only chromatin accessibility. This checks that the retained state causally changes output, as a memory element's stored value must when it is read.

ideas.title: Erase and rewrite perturbations with degron and dominant-negative AP-1
ideas.description: Add a degron or dominant-negative (e.g., A-Fos) at different times: during priming, only after washout, or at the time of the second challenge. If removing AP-1 after priming erases the memory, AP-1 is needed to maintain it. If removal only during priming blocks it, AP-1 is needed only to write it, and the memory is held elsewhere (e.g., histone marks or other TFs). Test whether re-pulsing resets the state.

ideas.title: Stress-testing durability with cycling, noise and division
ideas.description: Subject primed cells to repeated stimulation cycles, signaling noise (kinase inhibitor, fluctuating ligand), temperature or metabolic stress, and many cell divisions. Use live-cell AP-1 reporters in lineage-tracked single cells to measure how long the state lasts, how often it flips, and whether it is inherited by daughter cells. Fit a stochastic switching model to estimate memory half-life and robustness.
